explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The men from Bethel go to the priests of the house of the LORD of Hosts, and to the prophets too (Zechariah 7:3). They sent a whole delegation with their men, so this wasn't a casual question over the fence. When you've carried a question that far, you go straight to the people who speak for God.

Good guess if you're picturing a government office, but that's not where they go. The text says they ask the priests of the house of the LORD of Hosts, as well as the prophets (Zechariah 7:3). The governor never shows up in this verse. I think this question was too close to God's house to take anywhere else.

explanations.answer: The elders of their own town
explanations.explanation: Close to home, but that's not who they ask. The men sent from Bethel bring their question to the priests of the house of the LORD of Hosts and to the prophets (Zechariah 7:3). No town elders appear in these verses. They traveled to ask the ones at the house of the LORD.

Yep, that's what the LORD says. He tells Zechariah to ask all the people of the land and the priests (Zechariah 7:5). Notice that it's not only the priests. The question is for everybody. Nobody gets to sit this one out.

This one's actually true. The LORD says, "Ask all the people of the land and the priests…" (Zechariah 7:5). So the question goes to the whole crowd, not just one group. Nobody gets to dodge it, and I'd have been hiding behind the oven.

explanations.answer: Whether it was really for Him
explanations.explanation: That's it. God asks, "…was it really for Me that you fasted?" (Zechariah 7:5). Seventy years of fasting and mourning, and He puts one question on the table. It's not about the calendar. It's about who the fasting was for.

Nope, He never asks about length. The question is, "…was it really for Me that you fasted?" (Zechariah 7:5). Seventy years is already a long time, so the question isn't about how many days. It goes to who the fasting was for.

Not quite, friend. The priests aren't the ones doing the approving here. God asks the people, "…was it really for Me that you fasted?" (Zechariah 7:5). The question goes straight to the reason behind the fasting, and no committee is involved.

Right on. God says these are the words He proclaimed through the earlier prophets (Zechariah 7:7). Zechariah isn't bringing some brand new idea. The message was already out there, and God is pointing back to it.

Good thought, but the verse says something else. God proclaimed these words through the earlier prophets (Zechariah 7:7). Kings had plenty to say back then, but they aren't the ones named here. The words came through the prophets.

Easy one to grab, but no. The verse says the LORD proclaimed these words through the earlier prophets (Zechariah 7:7). Judges aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The messengers here are the prophets.

Let's check the verse, friend. It says Jerusalem and its surrounding towns were populous and prosperous, and the Negev and the foothills were inhabited (Zechariah 7:7). That's the opposite of empty. Back then the place was full of people.

Right. The verse says Jerusalem and its surrounding towns were populous and prosperous (Zechariah 7:7). The Negev and the foothills were inhabited too. So the places were busy, not empty. It's a lot like a bakery on cookie day, with every counter taken.
That's right. The LORD of Hosts says, "Administer true justice." (Zechariah 7:9). It's the first thing on the list. Straight, plain and no loopholes.

This one's actually true. The LORD of Hosts says, "Administer true justice." (Zechariah 7:9). It leads off His list of what to do. It's easy to miss when you're expecting a trick question, and I do it all the time.

That's the word. God says, "Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor." (Zechariah 7:10). He names four groups, so nobody can say they didn't know who He meant. To oppress means to press down on someone, and He says don't.

Not that one, friend. The verse says, "Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor." (Zechariah 7:10). The command isn't about being afraid of anyone. It's about not pressing down on people who already have less.

Close in sound, but no. The verse says, "Do not oppress the widow or the fatherless, the foreigner or the poor." (Zechariah 7:10). Oppress is a heavier word than blame. It means pressing down on someone, and God says don't do it to these four.

Let's look at what happens next. The verse says, "But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder…" (Zechariah 7:11). That's not paying attention. They had the message and they turned away from it.

Right. The text says they "refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder; they stopped up their ears from hearing." (Zechariah 7:11). That's three ways of saying no in one verse. These were not people leaning in to listen.

explanations.answer: Their hearts were hard and unbending
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says "They made their hearts like flint and would not listen…" (Zechariah 7:12). Flint is a hard stone, and you can't bend it. It's a picture of hearts that wouldn't give an inch. I've met dough like that on a cold morning, but this is much more serious.

explanations.answer: Their hearts were soft and easy to shape
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of flint, friend. The text says, "They made their hearts like flint and would not listen…" (Zechariah 7:12). Flint is a hard stone. Soft hearts would have listened, and these hearts did not.

explanations.answer: Their hearts were warm and wide open
explanations.explanation: Wide open would have been nice, but that's not the picture. The verse says they made their hearts like flint, and it says they would not listen (Zechariah 7:12). Flint is hard and doesn't bend. A flint heart is closed, not open.

Yes, and it's a heavy verse. The LORD says, "And just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen…" (Zechariah 7:13). The way they treated His call came back around. I think this is one of the hard parts to read, so take a breath with me.

That's not what the verse says, and it's a heavy one. The LORD says, "…just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen…" (Zechariah 7:13). He doesn't say He would answer at once. I think this is a hard line to read.

explanations.answer: He would send a new prophet
explanations.explanation: No new prophet in this verse, friend. The LORD says, "…just as I had called and they would not listen, so when they called I would not listen…" (Zechariah 7:13). It's a heavy line, and the verse leaves it at that.

explanations.answer: Among nations they had not known
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says He scattered them "with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known" (Zechariah 7:14). These were places they'd never seen. I think that's a hard place to land, far from everything familiar.

Not this time, friend. The verse says the LORD scattered them with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known (Zechariah 7:14). That's far beyond their own towns. It's a heavy verse, so no joke from me on this one.

explanations.answer: Out in the wilderness of Sinai
explanations.explanation: That's a famous spot, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says He scattered them "with a whirlwind among all the nations that they had not known" (Zechariah 7:14). The text points to nations, not to a wilderness. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it simple.

That's the word. The verse says "the land was left desolate behind them so that no one could come or go" (Zechariah 7:14). Desolate means empty and deserted. It's a sad picture of a land that used to be full.
Not guarded, friend. The verse says "the land was left desolate behind them so that no one could come or go" (Zechariah 7:14). Nobody is standing watch in this verse. The land was just left empty.

No water in this verse. It says "the land was left desolate behind them so that no one could come or go" (Zechariah 7:14). Desolate means empty and deserted. This is a sad verse, and a flood isn't part of it.
